title: Why We Need a Generalised Framework

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A generalised linear model (GLM) has three parts:

  1. A distribution for the outcome Y, given the predictors: Normal for a continuous outcome, binomial for a 0/1 outcome (recall §5.7.1.2), Poisson for a count (recall §5.7.1.3).
  2. A linear predictor, b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + …, exactly as in multiple regression (recall §12.4).
  3. A link function g that connects the two: g(μ) = b₀ + b₁x₁ + …, where μ is the expected value (mean) of Y.

Ordinary linear regression is itself a GLM: Normal distribution, identity link (g(μ) = μ). The other GLMs change the distribution, the link, or both. GLMs can therefore also handle continuous outcomes that are not Normal, such as skewed costs, but this book uses them for binary and count outcomes.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Fit a straight line to a 0/1 outcome and you meet a structural problem. A straight line runs to ±∞, but a probability must stay between 0 and 1. With enough spread in the predictor, the line will predict “probabilities” below 0 or above 1. Counts have the same problem at the bottom end: a line can predict −3 cases.

The GLM solution is to model a transformed mean that can take any value from −∞ to +∞, and transform back afterwards. For a probability the transformation is the logit (§13.2.2); for a count it is the natural logarithm (§13.5).

A GLM is not fitted by least squares. It is fitted by maximum likelihood. The likelihood of a set of parameter values is the probability of the data you actually observed, calculated as if those values were true. The maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) is the value that makes the observed data most probable. §15.1.1 develops likelihood further (model fit and comparison); here you need only the idea.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Toss a coin 10 times and get 7 heads. If the probability of a head is p, and tosses are independent (recall §5.4), the probability of this particular sequence is

L(p) = p⁷ (1 − p)³.

The log-likelihood is ln L = 7 ln p + 3 ln(1 − p). Its slope, found by calculus (beyond this book; the table below shows the peak numerically), is 7/p − 3/(1 − p). Setting the slope to zero gives 7(1 − p) = 3p, so p̂ = 7/10 = 0.7. The MLE is the sample proportion, which is what intuition says. For linear regression with Normal errors, maximising the likelihood gives exactly the least-squares estimates (recall §12.2.2). This is why the two methods agree for the identity-link GLM.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Fit a straight line by least squares to CBHI membership (1 = member, 0 = not) against the wealth index in the 500-household survey: predicted membership = 0.315 + 0.077 × wealth. For the poorest household (wealth −5.27) the line predicts 0.315 − 0.077 × 5.27 = −0.09, and six households get a negative “probability”. With a wider wealth range the line would also pass 1 at the top. These impossible predictions show that the straight line is the wrong model for this outcome.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
The likelihood of 7 heads in 10 tosses at five candidate values of p:

p L(p) = p⁷(1 − p)³ ln L
0.5 0.000977 −6.931
0.6 0.001792 −6.325
0.7 0.002224 −6.109
0.8 0.001678 −6.390
0.9 0.000478 −7.645

The likelihood peaks at p = 0.7. Software does the same search for every coefficient of a GLM at once.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cl <- read.csv("data/clinic_children.csv")
coef(lm(weight_kg ~ age_months, data = cl))
coef(glm(weight_kg ~ age_months, family = gaussian(link = "identity"),
          data = cl))
(Intercept)  age_months 
  8.4996278   0.1499948 
(Intercept)  age_months 
  8.4996278   0.1499948

glm with a Gaussian (Normal) family and identity link returns the same intercept (8.50 kg) and slope (0.150 kg per month) as lm on the 100 clinic children: linear regression is the identity-link GLM. Changing family is all it takes to move to logistic (binomial) or Poisson (poisson) regression.

points.html: Three parts: distribution, linear predictor, link. Linear regression = Normal distribution + identity link.

The coefficients act on the link scale. Each GLM needs its own back-transformation to give a readable measure: exp(b) is an odds ratio in logistic regression and a rate ratio in Poisson regression with an offset.
GLMs are fitted by maximum likelihood, not least squares. The two coincide for the Normal, identity-link case.
